title: The quiet time
hookLine: many Christians keep a morning quiet time: a Bible, a notebook, a coffee
last: A BRUISED REED HE WILL NOT BREAK.

lines: A BIBLE, A NOTEBOOK, A MUG.
cards: Six-fifteen in the morning. The house is still dark. A kettle clicks off.
Someone sits at the kitchen table with a mug and three things: a Bible with a cracked spine, a cheap notebook, a pen. No phone. Not yet.
They read a few verses, sit, write a line or two. Maybe a name they're worried about. Maybe a question.
Twenty minutes, sometimes ten, sometimes five. Then the day comes crashing in: kids, email, traffic. Christians in many places start their mornings something like this.

teach.h: A MODERN NAME, AN ANCIENT HABIT.
teach.b: The phrase is fairly recent, at home in evangelical churches and student groups. The habit is ancient. The Psalms are full of mornings.

teach.h: IN THE MORNING WILL I DIRECT MY PRAYER.
teach.b: Psalm five, in the King James Bible: "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up."
The Hebrew word for direct can mean to lay something out in order, like wood arranged for a fire, or a table set for a meal. The psalmist sets out the morning's prayer, then watches for an answer.

And Lamentations, a book of grief over a fallen city, still says of God's mercies: "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." That's the logic of first thing. You haven't failed at anything yet.
The day hasn't told you who you are. What happens varies, and that's fine. Some read a short passage, often following a plan.
Some write in a journal: what the verse said, what's on their mind, a prayer list.

teach.h: READ, WRITE, SIT, OR PRAY THE OFFICE.
teach.b: Catholics and Anglicans may pray morning prayer from the daily office, with psalms set for each day. Orthodox Christians may stand before icons at home and say the morning prayers. Some just sit in silence with coffee.
The common thread isn't the method.

teach.h: BEFORE THE WORLD GETS ITS SAY.
teach.b: It's the order: before the world gets its say, a little quiet gets the first word.
Nobody promises it will feel profound. Plenty of mornings are sleepy and blank. People keep it anyway, the way you keep a friendship: by showing up.

how: Many Christians keep a daily quiet time, often in the morning, reading a short Bible passage, writing in a journal and praying; others pray morning prayer from the daily office or say set morning prayers before icons at home.

practice: Open a notebook, a scrap of paper, or your phone's notes with everything else turned off, and write today's date and one honest line: what's on your mind right now.
Sit with it without fixing or polishing it, and add one more line if it comes. If you pray, write a name or a need and offer it; if not, let the page hold what you're carrying.
